summary:
Patricia of Oxylabs opens by framing infrastructure as the decisive layer for AI, since training alone is no longer enough and models need live retrieval. Oxylabs, founded in 2015, builds large-scale public web data extraction. Her first story: a sales team returned from San Francisco with a request for a video API for AI training on a two-week deadline at 5+ petabytes per month. The team built a dedicated scraper with new logic, storage integrations, and delivery flow on time. Client requests then cascaded: transcripts (failed — they actually needed subtitles), subtitle support, language-based search, and metadata. A one-off feature became a full video API suite. By 2026 the client had gathered 30 petabytes and the invoice is still outstanding. Lesson: clients buy the ability to adapt, not the first product iteration.

The second story covers SERP latency. Traditional search scraping averaged 4 seconds. A 2024 sub-second attempt was shelved because the market was not ready. In 2025 a new client required sub-second latency, zero data retention, and a two-week build. A redesign hit ~650 ms P90, but on the live demo call the system got blocked badly. Iteration two had to rely on browsers, which are slow, expensive, and incompatible with sub-second latency. There was no trick — only hunting for time across layouts, parsers, sessions, and proxies. The resulting Fast Search API averages 550 ms and now handles ~6 billion daily requests (up from 400 million).

The third story concerns scaling the web unblocker from 10,000 to 60,000 RPS in under two months. Each request means routing, rendering, proxy handling, browser execution, parsing, retries, normalization, and delivery. Load testing hit a wall around 20,000 RPS. Synthetic traffic was easy; organic-shaped traffic was hard. At scale, logs, metrics, and telemetry themselves become part of the load. Production traffic eventually validated the scaling. While scaling to 60k, demand shifted again: internally dubbed Project 60, it is already becoming Project 150 (100,000 RPS). The lesson is that scale is never a finish line; reaching one target number summons the next. Patricia concludes that Oxylabs is not just a proxy provider but the infrastructure layer that lets AI companies reach the open web, handle antibot systems, render browsers, normalize data, and deliver it into pipelines, databases, agents, and tools. Innovation, she argues, is the ability to keep adapting fast enough that changing requirements become new infrastructure. The next generation of AI will not be powered by better models but by better infrastructure around them.

sections.title: Infrastructure, not models, as the starting point
sections.summary: Patricia introduces Oxylabs (founded 2015) as a web intelligence and proxy platform. She argues training alone is no longer enough; models need fresh, live data, and that infrastructure layer is what decides whether AI is useful.

sections.title: A video API with a two week deadline
sections.summary: Sales returned from San Francisco with a request for a video API for AI training: two weeks, at least 5 petabytes per month. The team built a new dedicated scraper with fresh logic, storage, and delivery and made it on time, though the feature kept growing.

sections.title: Transcripts, subtitles, search, metadata
sections.summary: Client requests cascaded — transcripts failed because they actually meant subtitles; subtitle support was added; language-based search and metadata followed. In roughly three months a one-off feature became a full video API suite: downloaders, transcripts, subtitles, channel info, glued by an internal library.

sections.title: Thirty petabytes later, still unpaid
sections.summary: By 2026 the client had collected 30 petabytes of data and payment had still not arrived. Patricia's first lesson: clients buy the ability to adapt, not the first product iteration.

sections.title: A subsecond request, built and then shelved
sections.summary: SERP shifted from analytics/SEO into AI retrieval. A 2024 sub-second SERP attempt was built against a 4-second baseline but shelved because the market was not ready. In 2025 a new client demanded sub-second latency, zero data retention, and a two-week build.

sections.title: The rebuild, and getting blocked live on the call
sections.summary: A from-scratch redesign hit ~650 ms P90 in under two weeks, but during a live client demo call the system got blocked badly. Patricia distinguishes a system that works in development, one that passes tests, and one that survives reality. The team had to start over, relying on browsers, which are slow, expensive, and incompatible with sub-second targets.

sections.title: Hunting for time, second by second
sections.summary: There was no trick. The team hunted for milliseconds across layouts, parsers, sessions, and proxies, where small decisions accumulate. The Fast Search API now averages 550 ms and scales from 400 million to nearly 6 billion daily requests. Speed defines what product can exist.

sections.title: Scaling the unblocker to 60,000 per second
sections.summary: Demand forced scaling the web unblocker from 10,000 to 60,000 requests per second in under two months. Each request is an end-to-end scraping job — routing, rendering, proxy handling, browser execution, parsing, retries, normalization, delivery. Adding ~2,000 servers does not solve it; architecture, observability, and realistic testing are required.

sections.title: Load testing, and the wall at 20,000
sections.summary: The hardest part was not synthetic traffic but organic-shaped traffic. During a load test they hit a wall around 20,000 RPS. The system still worked, but uncertainty about whether it could go further became the real bottleneck, as metrics, logs, and processing at scale itself become part of the load. Observability at scale becomes real work.

sections.title: Observability as part of the load
sections.summary: Processing logs at scale is hard; metrics are essential but become part of the load and complexity. The team scaled gradually and accepted that real testing happens with production traffic, which fortunately went completely fine.

sections.title: Project 60 becomes Project 150
sections.summary: Internally dubbed Project 60 for the 60,000 RPS target, the effort is already becoming Project 150 as results approach 100,000 RPS. The lesson: scale is never a finish line; reaching one target number summons the next.

sections.title: Oxylabs as infrastructure, not just proxies
sections.summary: Patricia clarifies that Oxylabs is not just a proxy provider. Proxies matter, but the larger job is the infrastructure layer that lets companies extract public web data at scale — reaching the open web, handling antibot systems, rendering browsers when needed, normalizing, and delivering data so AI companies can plug it into their systems.

sections.title: Innovation as adapt forever
sections.summary: Patricia closes by redefining innovation as the ability to keep adapting fast enough that changing requirements become new infrastructure. Targets change, layouts change, detection changes, markets and client needs change — this is an adapt-forever business, not a build-once one. Her parting thought: the next generation of AI will not be powered by better models but by better infrastructure around them — infrastructure that connects models to reality, pushes web data into pipelines, databases, agents, and AI tools, and scales from 400 million to 6 billion daily requests. The model is not alone anymore; it already has a bridge to it.
